content: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are among the most common bacterial infections in infants, and acute pyelonephritis represents the most severe form of UTI. This condition can lead to significant acute illness and has the potential to cause permanent kidney damage. However, there is ongoing uncertainty regarding the optimal antibiotic regimen, including the choice of antibiotic, the route of administration, and the duration of treatment. This review is an update of previous reviews published in 2003, 2005, and 2007. The objective of this review was to assess the benefits and potential harms of various antibiotic treatments for children with acute pyelonephritis. Specifically, the review examined differences in antibiotic types, dosing regimens, treatment durations, and routes of administration. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Renal Group's Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, as well as reference lists and conference proceedings, up to April 10, 2014. There were no language restrictions applied. Randomised and quasi-randomised controlled trials involving children aged 0 to 18 years with confirmed UTI and acute pyelonephritis were included in the analysis. Four authors independently assessed the quality of the studies and extracted data. Statistical analyses were performed using a random-effects model, with results expressed as risk ratios (RR) for dichotomous outcomes or mean differences (MD) for continuous outcomes, along with 95% confidence intervals (CI). This updated review included 27 studies involving a total of 4,452 children. Three new studies were added, and one previously excluded study was re-evaluated and included. The risk of bias was assessed as low for sequence generation in 12 studies, allocation concealment in six studies, blinding of outcome assessors in 17 studies, incomplete outcome reporting in 19 studies, and selective outcome reporting in 13 studies. None of the studies blinded participants or investigators. The 27 studies evaluated 12 different comparisons. No significant differences were observed in the duration of fever (two studies, 808 children: MD 2.05 hours, 95% CI -0.84 to 4.94), the presence of persistent UTI at 72 hours after starting therapy (two studies, 542 children: RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.07 to 17.41), or the presence of persistent kidney damage at six to 12 months (four studies, 943 children: RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.12) between oral antibiotic therapy for 10 to 14 days and intravenous (IV) therapy for three days followed by oral therapy for 10 days. Similarly, no significant differences were found in persistent bacteriuria at the end of treatment (four studies, 305 children: RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.24 to 2.55) or persistent kidney damage (four studies, 726 children: RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.29) between IV therapy for three to four days followed by oral therapy and IV therapy for seven to 14 days. No significant differences in efficacy were observed between once-daily and thrice-daily administration of aminoglycosides (one study, 179 children, persistent clinical symptoms at three days: RR 1.98, 95% CI 0.37 to 10.53). Adverse events were mild, uncommon, and rarely led to discontinuation of treatment. The authors concluded that oral antibiotics alone are as effective as a short course (three to four days) of IV antibiotics followed by oral therapy for a total treatment duration of 10 to 14 days in treating acute pyelonephritis in children. When IV antibiotics are used, a short course (two to four days) of IV therapy followed by oral therapy is as effective as a longer course (seven to 10 days) of IV therapy. If aminoglycosides are chosen for IV therapy, single daily dosing is both safe and effective. However, there is insufficient data to apply these findings to children under one month of age or to those with dilating vesicoureteric reflux (grades III-V). Further research is needed to determine the optimal total duration of antibiotic therapy for acute pyelonephritis.
